meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Ideas are more powerful than guns. We would not let our enemies have guns, why should we let them have ideas?'?
meta.ogDescription: Pinned on Stalin everywhere, but no source shows he said it. It was a Usenet signature by 1995 and an unsourced anthology entry by 2001.

answer.label: Not Joseph Stalin — no known source
answer.authorDates: Online by February 1995 · in print by 2001
answer.sourceLine: No speech, article or letter by Stalin is known to contain this line. Wikiquote ↗ lists it as misattributed. It notes that the earliest source outside the blogosphere is Robert Torricelli’s 2001 anthology Quotations for Public Speakers, which gives no source. The line was already circulating as a Usenet signature in February 1995 ↗.

source.excerpt: “Ideas are more powerful than guns. We would not let our enemies have guns, why should we let them have ideas.” — Joseph Stalin
trail: No Stalin source. Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Stalin’s Misattributed quotes and says “there is not a single source which show that Stalin said this at any given time.”
1995 — a Usenet signature. The line, credited to “Joseph Stalin,” ends a ham-radio operator’s posts to rec.radio.amateur.misc from 16 February 1995 ↗ onward, and it reappears through April 1995 ↗.

2001 — an unsourced anthology. According to Wikiquote, the earliest source outside the blogosphere is former US senator Robert Torricelli’s Quotations for Public Speakers ↗ (Rutgers University Press, 2001), p. 121. The anthology does not say where the line came from.
Quote Investigator has not covered it. QI’s Stalin tag ↗ lists five other Stalin investigations, including “a single death is a tragedy” and the capitalists’ rope, but nothing on this line.
source.excerptNote: As it appears in a ham-radio operator’s Usenet signature dated 16 February 1995, the earliest copy this research found. The archive available covers only some newsgroups, so this shows the line was already circulating by that date. It is not the line’s origin, and it is not evidence that Stalin said it.

author.name: Joseph Stalin
author.heading: About Joseph Stalin
author.bio: Joseph Stalin (born Ioseb Jughashvili) was a Georgian revolutionary who led the Soviet Union from 1924 until his death in 1953 and ran it as a dictatorship. His regime’s censorship makes him an easy name to pin a line about banning ideas on. But this sentence has not been traced to any of his speeches or writings, and his collected Works are available to search ↗.

copyAttribution: “Ideas are more powerful than guns. We would not let our enemies have guns, why should we let them have ideas?” — commonly attributed to Joseph Stalin, but no source in his speeches or writings is known (Wikiquote lists it as misattributed). It circulated as a Usenet signature by February 1995 and appeared without a source in Robert G. Torricelli’s Quotations for Public Speakers (2001).

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Stalin
misattribution.intro: The line is a clean two-step syllogism about censorship, and that is why people attach it to Stalin. Every copy found traces back to quote lists rather than to anything Stalin wrote or said.

misattribution.truthLine: No Stalin speech, article or letter containing this line is known. Wikiquote finds no source, and its earliest known appearances are a 1995 Usenet signature and an unsourced 2001 anthology. Who first wrote it is unknown. See Wikiquote ↗

context.heading: Why it sticks
lead: The quote works as a gotcha. It puts a frank admission of censorship in the mouth of history’s best-known censor, and that makes it popular in arguments about speech, education and propaganda. It turns up in books, yearbooks, military papers and countless quote sites, always credited to Stalin and never with a source.

Its first sentence was already a stock phrase in Western Cold War rhetoric, where it meant the opposite of the Stalin version. A September 1952 issue of the U.S. Department of State Bulletin ↗ says that armies “have never been able to destroy ideas. In the long run, ideas are more powerful than guns.” The version credited to Stalin adds a sardonic second sentence that no one has traced to him.
context.pull: Armies have never been able to destroy ideas. In the long run, ideas are more powerful than guns. — Department of State Bulletin, 1952

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the quote under Stalin's Misattributed section, saying there is not a single source showing Stalin said it, and that the earliest source outside the blogosphere is Torricelli's Quotations for Public Speakers (2001), p. 121, which gives no source.
The line, credited to Joseph Stalin, appears as a Usenet signature in rec.radio.amateur.misc posts dated 16 February 1995.
The same signature line appears in rec.radio.amateur.misc posts in April 1995.
Quotations for Public Speakers: A Historical, Literary, and Political Anthology by Robert G. Torricelli was published by Rutgers University Press, New Brunswick, N.J., in 2001.
Quote Investigator's Joseph Stalin tag lists five investigations (votes, useful idiot, rope, funeral crowd, single death/statistic) and none on 'Ideas are more powerful than guns'.
A 2009 DTIC report uses the variant 'Ideas are far more powerful than guns. We don't allow our enemies to have guns, why should we allow them to have ideas?' credited to Joseph Stalin.
The September 1952 Department of State Bulletin contains: 'armies have never been able to destroy ideas. In the long run, ideas are more powerful than guns.'
The Marxists Internet Archive hosts Stalin's collected Works by volume.
Stalin was born 18 December 1878 and died 5 March 1953.
